title: Walking Borobudur
hookLine: pilgrims climb from carvings of desire to open terraces and a plain stupa at the top

lines: A NARROW GALLERY, WALLS OF STORIES.
cards: The first gallery of Borobudur is a narrow corridor, and the world shrinks. High stone walls rise on both sides: on your right, the carved panels of the main wall; on your left, the balustrade, carved too.
Overhead, only a strip of sky. You walk, and read, and turn the corner, and walk again. Princes, palaces, hermits, animals, crowds.
Then a stairway, and another gallery just like it, and another. Hours can pass in here. Then, near the top, you climb one more flight, and the walls are simply gone.
Wind. Light. Open terraces, round instead of square, and the volcano on the horizon.

teach.h: AT THE BASE: DEEDS AND THEIR RESULTS.
teach.b: First, the bottom. At the very base of Borobudur is a hidden foot, a ring of carvings later covered over with stone.
They show deeds and their results: people quarreling, hunting, gossiping, giving alms, and what each brings in its turn. Daily life, wanting and its fruit, is where the climb starts.

Second, the galleries. Above that come the square, walled corridors: the Buddha's life, his past lives, and the long journey of a young seeker named Sudhana, who goes from teacher to teacher looking for the way.
You can't see out. All you can see is story.
Third, the open terraces. Then the walls end. The top levels are round and plain, with no carved scenes at all.
Rows of stupas stand there, each one a stone lattice, like a bell made of open diamonds, and inside each sits a Buddha you can just glimpse through the gaps. Fourth, the top.

teach.h: AT THE TOP: ONE PLAIN STUPA AND SKY.
teach.b: In the middle stands one large, plain stupa, closed, and around it is nothing but sky.

One reading, offered by scholars and guides, sees three Buddhist realms in the climb: the realm of desire at the base, the realm of form in the carved galleries, and the formless realm on the open terraces.
Whether or not the builders drew it that neatly, the change is there in the walking: crowded pictures, then fewer, then none at all. The stories carry you up, and then they let you go.

how: Pilgrims walk Borobudur from the bottom up, circling each level clockwise before climbing to the next, and at the Vesak festival monks and lay Buddhists process there with candles and chanting.

o: a pilgrims' race up the stairs at dawn
a dance performed around a great stupa
the climb from carved stories to open sky

p: the life, past lives, Sudhana's search

s: the top of Borobudur is covered in the busiest carvings
the top terraces are plain; the carving thins out as you climb.
Buddhas sit inside the lattice stupas on the round terraces
you can just glimpse them through the gaps.
the carvings at the very base show deeds and their results
quarrels, hunting, gossip, giving, and what each brings.

games.q: you've walked every gallery of Borobudur, through walls of stories, and you climb the last stairs to the very top. what's waiting there?
o: a huge golden statue of the Buddha.
one plain, closed stupa and open sky.
the grandest carved scene of the awakening.
games.why: at the top there are no pictures at all: one large, plain stupa, ringed by lattice stupas, and sky. the stories carry you up, then let you go.

practice: If there are stairs near you, climb them slowly, and if not, a single step, a doorway or your imagination will do, letting the weight come onto each foot before the next.
Let your thoughts be as busy as the carved walls on the way up, let them thin out near the top, and at the last step stop, with just air and breath.

wordCard.voice: Walking Borobudur. The pilgrim's climb: from carved deeds at the base, through walled galleries of story, to open terraces and one plain stupa under the sky. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the realm of desire, which one reading places at Borobudur's base.

carryVoice: Your line: from carvings to open sky. The busiest walls come first, and the sky comes last. Day eight hundred ninety-one, done.
